user_locked: Reference video 1 is used for motion imitation; the three suit-wearing men in it are replaced by three highly realistic capybaras.
Camera stays fixed: the original position, angle and wide full-shot framing are kept unchanged for the whole clip, with no cuts.

Capybara motion must strictly follow the source trajectory: all three drop prone to the floor in rapid succession; the leftmost capybara jumps to the middle position; the capybara in the middle rolls to the leftmost; the capybara in the middle then rolls to the rightmost; the rightmost capybara jumps to the middle; finally the middle capybara jumps onto the backs of the other two and they stack into a pyramid.
Photorealistic capybara fur texture, with lighting that merges the animals into the source environment.

content_events.text: Replace the three suit-wearing men in video_1 with three highly realistic capybaras occupying the same positions and roles.
The three capybaras drop prone onto the floor in rapid succession until all three lie flat.
The leftmost capybara jumps to the middle position while the capybara in the middle rolls to the leftmost position.
The capybara now in the middle rolls to the rightmost position while the rightmost capybara jumps to the middle.
The middle capybara jumps onto the backs of the other two and the three stack into a pyramid that holds to the end.
The capybaras reproduce video_1's full-body motion trajectory, action ordering and performance timing, including the final stacked-pyramid end state.

audio_requirements.text: Audio is generated for the clip; no dialogue, no music and no source-audio reuse are requested. Sounds must match the visible action: wooden-floor impacts for each prone landing, fur-and-paw scrapes as the bodies move across the boards, and one heavier impact for the final stack.

must_keep: Exactly three capybaras replacing the three suited men, occupying the same left, middle and right floor positions.

The motion order: successive prone drops, then the left-to-middle jump with the middle rolling left, then the middle rolling right with the right jumping to the middle, then the middle capybara jumping onto the backs of the other two.
The final stacked pyramid (two prone bodies as the base, one balanced on top) held until the last frame.
Fixed camera: same position, angle and wide full-shot framing from first frame to last, with no cuts and no camera movement.
Photorealistic capybara fur and lighting integrated with the wooden-floor environment and its shadow direction.

shots.content_purpose: Single locked-off wide take showing the whole capybara routine in the unchanged framing and lighting of <Video 1>: the standing line, the rapid prone drops, the two left/middle/right position exchanges and the final stacked pyramid held to the last frame.
shots.description:
The camera holds the same fixed wide full shot as <Video 1>, its position, angle, height and framing identical from the first frame to the last; it never pans, tilts, zooms, pushes or shakes. The light-brown polished wooden floor with white circular markings and the unchanged ambient lighting of the source fill the frame, and the whole routine follows <Video 1>'s performance timing across the 5.875 seconds, the prone drops, the two position exchanges and the final stack succeeding one another at the source's pace. In place of the three suited men, <Subject 1>, <Subject 2> and <Subject 3> stand on the floor in the same left, middle and right positions and at the same distance from the camera as the source figures, all three fully inside the frame; their brown fur, its density and its specular sheen respond to the same overhead light that falls on the source figures, and each body casts a soft contact shadow onto the wood. The woman in white standing at the left of the frame stays in place, motionless and clear of the animals.
The three capybaras then drop prone onto the floor in rapid succession, starting from the left: <Subject 1> flops flat on its belly first, immediately followed by <Subject 2> and then <Subject 3>, each landing with its short legs tucked under its barrel body and its fur compressing against the polished wood, a dull wooden thud and a short fur-and-paw scrape sounding at each landing. All three end lying low and flat in their original left, middle and right positions, facing the camera.
Without standing up, <Subject 1> hops sideways across the floor into the middle position while <Subject 2> rolls left along the boards into the emptied left position, both bodies staying low through the exchange. Then the capybara now in the middle, <Subject 1>, rolls rightward over the wood into the right position while <Subject 3> jumps from the right into the middle, leaving <Subject 2> prone on the left, <Subject 3> prone in the middle and <Subject 1> prone on the right.
In the final part of the shot, <Subject 3> springs up from the middle and lands across the backs of the two prone capybaras flanking it, <Subject 2> on the left and <Subject 1> on the right, so the three animals form the stacked pyramid that ends <Video 1>: two flat bodies as the base with the third balanced on top of both. A heavier, softer impact marks the landing, the top capybara settles with its fur still moving from the impact, and the pyramid holds inside the unchanged frame until the last frame.

uncertainties: The reference video's audio track was not analysed (no audio evidence was supplied) and no audio reuse was requested, so no source audio is copied; overall_soundscape is synthesised from the visible action only.

The user did not specify whether the woman in white standing to the left of the three figures (person_4 in the analysis) should be kept or removed; she is retained as a stationary bystander, which can be changed if unwanted.

The supplied analysis describes the source only as crouching/dropping to the floor, a roll and a pyramid, and does not confirm the two left/middle/right position exchanges the user described; the prompt follows the user's stated sequence as authoritative.
The initial prone drops are written as a rapid left-to-right cascade, an inference from "依次"; the evidence does not confirm the order.
How a quadruped capybara performs the "jump" and "roll" beats while staying low to the floor is an interpretation, since the source shows bipedal humans.
Five action beats inside 5.875 s are very tight; if a beat stretches or is dropped, the final pyramid may not resolve before the clip ends.
